explanation:
## Three signatures, three contracts

```cpp
long long total(const std::vector<int>& v);   // reads
void addToAll(std::vector<int>& v, int d);    // writes
void reverseIt(std::vector<int>& v);          // writes
```

The signature is documentation the compiler checks. A caller looking at `total`
knows its vector will not change, and not because a comment says so - add
`v.push_back(1)` inside `total` and the build fails with "no matching member
function for call to push_back", because on a `const` vector only the
const-qualified members are callable.

That is the real value of `const`. It is not a performance hint; it is a
constraint, and the compiler is the one enforcing it.

## Why `const&` rather than by value

```cpp
long long total(std::vector<int> v)          // copies every element
long long total(const std::vector<int>& v)   // copies nothing
```

A `std::vector` owns a heap allocation holding its elements. Copying one
allocates new storage and copies every element - so passing a thousand-element
vector by value is a thousand copies plus a `new`, to compute a sum that reads
each element once.

A reference is just an address under the hood, so passing by reference is one
machine word regardless of how big the thing is.

The rule of thumb from the Core Guidelines: **take `const&` for anything you only
read and that is not cheap to copy.** For `int`, `double` or a pointer, by value
is cheaper than a reference and reads better. For strings, vectors, maps and
anything holding an allocation, `const&`.

## Accumulating into the wider type

```cpp
long long s{};
for (int x : v) s += x;
```

`s += x` promotes `x` to `long long` before adding, because that is the type of
the left side. So the addition itself happens in 64 bits and there is no
intermediate that could overflow.

The wrong version is subtler than it looks:

```cpp
int s{};                                        // overflows
for (int x : v) s += x;
return s;                                       // widened too late
```

The widening to `long long` on return happens *after* the damage. Two values of
two billion each sum to four billion, which does not fit in a 32-bit `int`, and
signed overflow is undefined behaviour - so the result is not "wrapped to a
negative number you can predict", it is a program the standard gives no meaning
to. At `-O2`, GCC is entitled to assume the overflow cannot happen and optimise
accordingly.

The hidden cases include sums of ±8 billion precisely to make the right type
necessary rather than merely tidy.

## Modifying through a reference, at both levels

```cpp
void addToAll(std::vector<int>& v, int d)
{
    for (int& x : v) x += d;
}
```

Two references are needed and each one matters:

- `std::vector<int>& v` so the function works on the caller's vector
- `int& x` so each loop iteration works on the vector's element

Drop either `&` and the function compiles and does nothing observable. Drop the
first and you modify a copy of the vector; drop the second and you modify a copy
of each element. Neither is an error - both are legal programs that mean
something else - which is why "my function did not change anything" is almost
always a missing `&`.

## Reversing in place

```cpp
std::size_t i{ 0 };
std::size_t j{ v.size() };
while (i + 1 < j) { std::swap(v[i], v[j - 1]); ++i; --j; }
```

The same two-index walk as the palindrome check, swapping instead of comparing.
`j` is one-past-the-end for the same reason: `v.size() - 1` on an empty vector
underflows `std::size_t` to an enormous number, because it is unsigned.

In real code this is one line:

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
std::reverse(v.begin(), v.end());
```

which is shorter, cannot be off by one, and says what it does. Writing it by
hand once is worth it to see that a reverse is n/2 swaps and touches no extra
memory.

## Printing without a trailing space

`printAll` prints the label first, then a space *before* each element. The label
absorbs the separator problem: there is always something before the first value,
so no flag is needed and an empty vector prints just the label.

That is why the label is part of the function rather than printed by the caller -
a small design choice that removes a special case.

## `const char*` for the label

```cpp
void printAll(const char* label, const std::vector<int>& v)
```

`const char*` is a pointer to characters, which is what a string literal like
`"after-add"` actually is. `const std::string&` would also work and would
construct a `std::string` at each call. For a literal, the pointer is the
natural fit; `std::string_view` is the modern answer that accepts both with no
copy either way.
